blocks.text: Alas! What scorpion within, what crab, turned back and fixed in me with burning wound, scorches my marrow? — — —
See the rest there, and more on the same theme in Sophocles, in the Trachiniae, where even the fleece dyed with this poison is eaten away and consumed as if by a hidden fire ^{e)}:
Τοῦτ' ἠφάνισαι διάβορον πρὸς οὐδενὸς Τῶν ἔνδων, ἀλλ' ἐδεστὸν ἐξ αὐτοῦ φθίνει. [Tout' ēphanisai diaboron pros oudenos Tōn endōn, all' edeston ex autou phthinei.] [col. 423]
Although these things are exaggerated, as is the custom of poets, they nevertheless show abundantly that the name שרף saraph, that is, ἐμπρηστοῦ [emprēstou], suits this evil most of all.

But what moves me above all to believe that שרף saraph is the hydrus is that I see Egypt called in Es. XXX, 6. the land from which comes the viper, ושרף מעופף, and the flying Saraph: namely the winged serpents which, as Cicero ^{f)} and Josephus ^{g)} write, fly into Egypt from Libya; as Herodotus ^{h)}, Mela ^{i)}, Lucan ^{k)}, Solinus ^{l)}, Ammianus ^{m)} write, from Arabia; and as Aelian writes, from both regions ^{n)}. These had the appearance of hydri ^{(1)}. The matter is stated explicitly in Herodotus ^{o)}: Τοῦ δ' ὄφιος ἡ μορφὴ, οἵηπερ τῶν ὕδρων [Tou d' opheos hē morphē, hoiēper tōn hydrōn]; The form of the serpent is like that of the hydri. To this belongs the fact that Cicero calls them angues [snakes], that is, water serpents. And Lucilius, book 23,

— — portents, and winged snakes. [III, 214] So also Solinus and Ammianus, who likewise, following Mela, report that they emerge from marshes. So it is now plain to everyone that the kind of winged serpents belongs to the species of the hydri. You will ask where Isidore gets the statement that they are called Sirens. In Arabia, he says, there are serpents with wings, which are called Sirens, which not only run faster than horses but are even said to fly. Someone might think this an Arabic word. But in the writings of the Arabs I have found only two names for winged serpents, very far removed from this one: namely سف [sf] and اعرجات [aʿrajāt]. And what this is will be told in the chapter On the Dragon.
If there should be anyone who, with the Hebrews, thinks that the flying saraph in Isaiah is the acontias, and that by flight nothing but a leap is meant, in the sense in which Lucan said,

as though what we read in the ancients about winged snakes were fables, let him know that the fact is confirmed by many in our age: and that in France itself, among the Bigerrones by the Pyrenees, there is a kind of snake from whose sides cartilages spread out in the manner and appearance of wings. So Scaliger against Cardano, Exercitation 183. And Brodaeus, Miscellanea, book 3, chapter 1, records one in the territory of the Santones struck down by a peasant's hoe as it flew at him, and presented to King Francis. Cardano too, De Varietate rerum, book 7, chapter 29, writes that he saw in Paris five two-footed serpents with tiny wings, but brought from India; in which country Megasthenes had long ago described winged snakes, in Aelian, book 16, chapter 41. And Odoardo Barbosa, treating of the mountain that divides Malabar and Narsinga: Vi si trouano serpe con ali, molto velenose, che volano: delli quali è fama, che col fiato è la guardatura ammazano, quei che vi, si pongono troppo appresso. That is, There winged and flying serpents are found, very poisonous, which are reported to kill with their breath and gaze those who come too near. Scaliger copied this almost word for word against Cardano, Exercitation 183, chapter 5. And Vincent le Blanc, Part 1 of the Travels, chapter 25: East of Lake Chiamay there are great forests and vast marshes, to which the journey is dangerous, because very large serpents live there which, lifted from the ground as if by bats' wings and supported on the tip of their tail, are carried along very swiftly. They say these once existed in such numbers around these places that they almost depopulated the neighbouring province. And below: I saw some of them of immense bulk, which, when hungry, attack sheep and other cattle ^{(2)}.

[III, 215] I cannot help adding that the flying saraph is placed by the Hebrews among those animals whose odour is noxious. Porta Coeli fol. 24. a. b.: ויש מקצת בעלי חיים שיצא ארס גדול וריח רע וחזק מפיהם כמין זאב ומין שרף מעופף, And there are certain animals from whose mouth comes much poison and a bad and heavy odour, such as the wolf and the flying saraph. And again: ושרף מעופף שורף האויר המעפש ההוא כל קרוב אליו, And the flying saraph, scorching the air, infects everything that is near it. [col. 424] From this a new argument arises to prove that the saraph belongs to the kind of the hydri. For of them the greatest Poet says,
